0.title: More Than Spoons and Tables
0.essay:
Many Christians set out to read the Bible from cover to cover and stall somewhere in Exodus or Leviticus. The rescue from Egypt is gripping. Then come chapter after chapter of curtains, frames, rings, poles, bowls, bulls and goats. One reader put the question honestly: is it just the spoon and the table and the this and the that? Or is a Christian allowed to see something of Christ and the gospel in all these details?

Who this study is for

It is for anyone who has felt that puzzlement: the new Christian who wonders why so much of the Old Testament is about animals and furniture, the long-time believer who quietly skips the second half of Exodus, and the Bible-study leader who wants to teach these chapters without either skating over them or making them say what they do not say. You need no Hebrew. Each unit tries first to help you picture the thing itself. These chapters were read aloud to shepherds and their children, who walked past the altar every day and smelled the smoke. God meant ordinary people to understand them.

Three steps

Every unit takes three steps. First, what it was for Israel: what it looked like, what was done with it, and what it taught. Second, how it points to Christ: how the New Testament shows it fulfilled in his person and work. Third, what it means for us now.

The short answer to the reader’s question is yes. The Christian may see Christ here, and should, because Jesus taught his disciples to read these books that way. But there is a careful way and a careless way to do it. Unit 1 sets out three levels: links named in the New Testament, links consistent with the New Testament, and speculation to avoid. Throughout the study we say which level we are on, so that you can tell what God has said from what Christians have guessed.

Other studies in this commentary stand alongside this one: The Big Story of the Bible, Covenant Theology, God with His People and Christ in the Old Testament. Here we stay close to what puzzles readers most: the furniture, the priests, the offerings, the festivals, the laws, and how to read the stories and poems.

The chapters

Can a Christian See Christ in the Details?; The Tabernacle: God Living Among His People; The Courtyard: The Bronze Altar and the Basin; The Holy Place: Lamp, Bread and Incense; The Most Holy Place: The Ark and the Mercy Seat; From Tent to Temple; Priests, Levites and the High Priest; The Five Offerings; The Day of Atonement; Clean and Unclean, and the Food Laws; The Feasts: Passover to Pentecost; The Autumn Feasts, the Sabbath and the Jubilee; The Law and the Christian; The Hard Laws; Reading the Stories Well; and Poetry, Prophecy and Wisdom.

For reflection

Which part of the Old Testament have you found hardest to read, and why? Have you ever been told that some detail “stands for” Christ and wondered how anyone could know? What would you most like to understand by the end of this study?

1.title: Can a Christian See Christ in the Details?
1.essay:
On the evening of the first Easter Sunday two disciples walked to Emmaus, sad and confused. A stranger joined them, and before they reached home he had given them the most remarkable Bible study ever taught: “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). The stranger was the risen Jesus, and his subject was himself.

Jesus taught us to read this way

Later he told the apostles that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). “The Law of Moses” means the first five books of the Bible, the very books that contain the tabernacle, the priests and the sacrifices. To the scholars of his day he said, “For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (John 5:46).

So we are not being fanciful when we look for Christ in Exodus and Leviticus. The apostles followed him. Paul says Israel’s food laws, festivals and Sabbaths “are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). Of Israel in the wilderness he writes, “these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Copy, shadow and type

Hebrews gives us the key words. Israel’s priests “serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and the law has “but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities” (Hebrews 10:1). A shadow falls across the path before someone turns the corner. It is real and has the right shape, but it is not the person, and when he appears nobody goes on staring at the shadow.

The New Testament word for such a pattern is typos, from which we get “type”. A type is a real person, event or institution in Israel’s history that God designed to prefigure something greater in Christ. The Passover lamb was a real lamb, killed on a real night; it was also a type of “Christ, our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). A type is not a code but God shaping history so that, when the reality came, people would recognise him. And the fulfilment is always greater: a lamb that saved one household for one night pointed to the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world.

Three levels

Not every link Christians have made is equally sure, so this study uses three levels. Level one: named in the New Testament. These are firm, because God himself has drawn the line. The mercy seat on the ark is the place of propitiation, and Paul uses the same word of Christ (Romans 3:25). The curtain before the Most Holy Place stands for Christ’s flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). The tabernacle points to the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Christ is the Passover lamb, the great high priest, the bread from heaven, the light of the world; the temple is his body and his church. Incense is the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8). The bronze serpent pictures the Son of Man lifted up on the cross (John 3:14).

Level two: consistent with the New Testament. These are fair inferences from the plain meaning of the Old Testament in the light of the New, offered as such. The bronze altar stood first, at the entrance: no one comes to God except through sacrifice. The basin fits the New Testament’s language of washing. The bread eaten by the priests in God’s house fits the Lord’s Table. The courtyard had one gate. None is stated in so many words, but each follows the grain of what the New Testament says.

Level three: speculation to avoid. Some readers have found a meaning in every colour, metal, number and material: the acacia wood is Christ’s humanity, the gold his deity, the badger skins his plain appearance, the number of loops on the curtains a hidden truth. Where Scripture itself does not give such meanings, we must not make them doctrine.

Why the guard rails matter

Take the “badger skins” of the King James Version, on which sermons were built. Modern translations render the same Hebrew word as “goatskins” (Exodus 26:14), and others suggest the hide of a sea creature such as the dugong. Nobody is sure. A doctrine resting on that word rests on sand. The writer to the Hebrews, who understood the tabernacle better than anyone, lists its furniture and then stops himself: “Of these things we cannot now speak in detail” (Hebrews 9:5). That restraint is a model for us.

Church history teaches the same lesson. Origen of Alexandria, in the third century, loved Christ and the Scriptures, but taught that a text’s deepest meaning often lay hidden beneath its plain sense, and his followers found hidden meanings almost everywhere. In the Middle Ages this grew into a fourfold method, in which one verse could carry a literal, an allegorical, a moral and a heavenly sense. The Reformers pushed back. Luther, Tyndale and Calvin insisted that a passage has one true sense, its plain, natural meaning, and that we find Christ by following that sense to its goal, not by escaping it. The Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession agree: the true sense of a passage is one, not many, and Scripture interprets Scripture. Some popular nineteenth-century writers on the tabernacle drifted back into finding a lesson in every board and peg. They meant well, and said true things about Christ, but from texts that do not teach them.

Devotional reflections on small details are not wicked. A believer may look at the pure gold of the lampstand and think of the purity of Christ. That is fine, if it is held lightly and never preached as what the text means. The test is simple: does Scripture say so, or does it plainly follow from what Scripture says?

An example

A woman leading a Bible study on Exodus felt she had to find Christ in every verse, and her group grew bored or bewildered by her explanations of the tent pegs. A friend suggested three questions for each passage: what did this mean for Israel, where does the New Testament take it, and what does it mean for us? Her studies became shorter, clearer and fuller of Christ, because she spent her time on what God had actually said.

For reflection

What difference does it make that Jesus himself taught his disciples to read Moses as speaking of him? How would you explain the difference between a type and an allegory? Have you been taught a meaning in some Old Testament detail that you now think was speculation? How can the three levels help you read with both confidence and humility?

2.title: The Tabernacle: God Living Among His People
2.essay:
The Ten Commandments get one chapter of Exodus. The tabernacle gets thirteen, told twice, first as instructions and then as the record of the building. A modern reader may wonder why. But think how much space a love letter might give to the home the couple will share. God was telling his people where he was going to live: among them.

Why a tent?

God gave the reason in one sentence: “And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8). He had brought Israel out of Egypt “that I might dwell among them” (Exodus 29:46). The exodus was not only a rescue from slavery. It was a rescue for fellowship.

The dwelling was a tent because the people lived in tents, and God chose to travel with them. The Hebrew word for tabernacle, mishkan, comes from the verb “to dwell”. The God of heaven and earth pitched his tent in the middle of a camp of former slaves, among the cooking fires and the flocks.

Walking in from the east

Picture the camp from a hill. The twelve tribes are camped in a great square, three on each side, all facing inwards (Numbers 2:2). Closer in, the Levites’ tents form a guard. In the centre stands a fence of white linen, a hundred cubits by fifty, about 46 metres by 23, and more than two metres high (Exodus 27:18). There is one way in, a wide embroidered gate on the east side.

Go through the gate. Before you is a bronze altar with smoke rising from it, and beyond it a bronze basin of water. Beyond those stands the tent itself: upright frames of acacia wood overlaid with gold, covered with layers of curtains and skins. It had two rooms. The first, the Holy Place, held a golden lampstand, a golden table with bread, and a small golden altar for incense. The second, behind a thick curtain, was the Most Holy Place, probably a cube about four and a half metres each way, holding only the ark of the covenant. Units 3, 4 and 5 walk through each in turn.

The further in you go, the holier the ground and the fewer the people allowed. Any Israelite could come to the gate with an offering. Only priests entered the Holy Place. Only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year. The floor plan itself preached that God is near, and that God is holy.

Echoes of Eden

The tabernacle also looks back. In Eden God walked with man (Genesis 3:8). After the fall, “at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). Now God makes a dwelling entered from the east, with cherubim woven into its inner curtains and into the veil before the inner room (Exodus 26:1, 31). The way to God was still guarded, but now there was a way, through sacrifice. Many readers also notice that the lampstand was shaped like a flowering tree, and that gold and onyx, named in the description of Eden (Genesis 2:12), adorned the high priest. These echoes are level two. The Bible begins in a garden where God lives with his people and ends in a garden city where he does so for ever (Revelation 22:1–2). The tabernacle is a small, portable Eden on the way.

Made by the pattern

Israel did not design the tabernacle. God told Moses, “Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it” (Exodus 25:9). Hebrews explains why: the earthly tent was a copy of a heavenly reality (Hebrews 8:5). We do not decide how sinners may approach a holy God; he tells us. So Exodus 40 repeats seven times that each thing was done “as the LORD had commanded Moses” (Exodus 40:23).

Yet the God who gave the pattern also gave the skill. Of Bezalel, the chief craftsman, God said, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Bezalel is the first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and the filling was for craftsmanship. Ordinary Israelites gave the gold, yarn and skins, each one “whose heart moves him” (Exodus 25:2), so freely that Moses had to tell them to stop (Exodus 36:6).

The glory came down

When all was finished, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). The study God with His People traces this moment and what followed. Notice the last verse of Exodus: the cloud by day and fire by night stayed over the tent “in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys” (Exodus 40:38). God did not visit and leave. He stayed, and he moved when they moved.

The Word pitched his tent

Here is level one. John writes, “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The Greek verb for “dwelt” comes from the word for a tent: the Word pitched his tent among us. The God who lived in a tent of goat hair and linen came to live in a tent of human flesh, and the glory that once filled the tabernacle was seen in a man. The tabernacle was never the goal. It was a promise in fabric that God would one day come closer still.

And the story goes on. At the end of the Bible a loud voice says, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). The word for dwelling place is again the tent word. The God who camped with Israel in the wilderness will live with his people for ever.

What it means for us

The tabernacle tells us what God is like. He wants to live with his people, and he has gone to astonishing lengths to do it. He is also holy, and the way in is his way, not ours. And he gives both the pattern and the power for his work: the gifts you bring to his people, however practical, can be the work of his Spirit.

A carpenter who had always felt his skills were not spiritual read Exodus 31 at a men’s breakfast. He had never noticed that the first man said to be filled with the Spirit was a craftsman. He began giving a Saturday a month to repairs in the homes of elderly church members, and found that the work felt like worship.

For reflection

What does it tell you about God that he wanted to live in the middle of Israel’s camp? How does the layout of the tabernacle show both his nearness and his holiness? What does John 1:14 add to your picture of Christ when you remember the tabernacle? How might your own skills be used in God’s service?

3.title: The Courtyard: The Bronze Altar and the Basin
3.essay:
Walk through the gate of the tabernacle courtyard and the first thing to meet you is not gold or beauty. It is heat, smoke, the smell of burning fat, and blood. It was meant to be shocking, and the shock was meant to teach.

The one gate

The courtyard had one entrance, a screen twenty cubits wide, about nine metres, “of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework” (Exodus 27:16). It was wide, but it was the only way in. Jesus never calls himself the tabernacle gate, but he does say, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9), and “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). So the single gate is level two, a fair picture: there is one way to God, and it is wide open to all who come by it.

The bronze altar

Just inside stood the altar of burnt offering, a hollow box of acacia wood covered with bronze, five cubits square and three high (Exodus 27:1), about two and a quarter metres square and chest high. A horn stuck up at each corner. A bronze grating halfway down held the fire, and poles let the Levites carry it.

Every morning and every evening a year-old lamb was offered whole, with flour, oil and wine (Exodus 29:38–42). Through the day Israelites brought their own offerings (see Unit 8). The worshipper laid his hand on the animal’s head and killed it; the priests caught the blood in bowls and threw it against the altar or smeared it on the horns. Then the fire did its work. And the fire never went out: “Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out” (Leviticus 6:13). God himself had lit it, when “fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering” (Leviticus 9:24).

Why blood? God explained: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls” (Leviticus 17:11). Sin deserves death. At the altar a life was given in place of the sinner’s. Every Israelite met this truth first: there is no approach to a holy God except through a death in your place.

The altar had its own bronze tools: “pots for it to receive its ashes, and shovels and basins and forks and fire pans” (Exodus 27:3). The pots were buckets for ash; the shovels scraped the grating; the basins caught and threw the blood; the forks were long hooks for arranging meat on the fire; the fire pans carried live coals. We need not hunt for a hidden meaning in each. They were the working tools of a holy kitchen, made by God’s pattern and set apart for his house (see Unit 4).

The basin

Between the altar and the tent stood a bronze basin on a bronze stand, filled with water. Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet there before entering the tent or serving at the altar, “so that they may not die” (Exodus 30:21). Scripture gives no measurements for it, but it tells us where the bronze came from: “from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting” (Exodus 38:8). Women who served gave up their polished mirrors, and they became the place where the priests were made clean.

The order matters. First the altar, then the basin, then the tent. First atonement, then cleansing, then fellowship. Even those accepted by sacrifice could not walk into God’s presence with the dirt of the road on them.

Fulfilled in Christ

Hebrews says, “We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat” (Hebrews 13:10), and at once explains that the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). That is level one. The altar where God’s fire fell on a substitute finds its meaning at the cross, where Christ bore the judgment our sins deserve.

Hebrews draws another contrast: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down” (Hebrews 10:11–12). Among all the tabernacle’s furniture there was no chair. The priests’ work was never finished, and the fire never went out because the sins never stopped. Christ sat down, because his work was done.

The basin points to cleansing. Hebrews urges us to draw near “with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22), language that recalls priests at the altar and the basin. Paul speaks of “the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). Taking the basin as a picture of this is level two. Jesus’ words to Peter fit it closely: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean” (John 13:10). The priests were washed all over once, at their ordination (Exodus 29:4), and then washed hands and feet daily. The believer is washed once for all in the new birth, and then comes daily for cleansing from the dust of the road: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

What it means for us

The courtyard tells us to begin where God begins. We do not come to him by our good intentions or sincerity, but by the altar, by the death of Christ in our place. Then we are free to come daily for cleansing, without fear, because the one great sacrifice has been made.

A man who had been a Christian for years still felt he had to make himself presentable before he could pray: a good day, a clear conscience, some progress to report. When he read about the altar standing first at the gate, he saw that he had it backwards. Israel did not tidy themselves up and then come to the altar. They came because they were not clean. He began to start his prayers where the tabernacle starts, with thanks for the cross.

For reflection

Why do you think God placed the altar first, right inside the gate? What does the fire that never went out tell you about sin, and what does Christ sitting down tell you about his work? How does the basin help you understand both your once-for-all washing and your daily need of cleansing? Where are you tempted to clean yourself up before coming to God?

4.title: The Holy Place: Lamp, Bread and Incense
4.essay:
Step through the curtain at the front of the tent and the noise and smoke of the courtyard fall away. You are in a room about nine metres long and four and a half wide, with no windows. The walls gleam with gold, and the ceiling curtain is woven with cherubim. Three pieces of furniture stand there, with a few small golden tools. This was the Holy Place, where the priests served daily. Why should a Christian care about a lamp, a table and a little altar?

The lampstand

On the left as you entered, on the south side (Exodus 40:24), stood the lampstand: not a candlestick but a stand for seven oil lamps, hammered from a single block of pure gold weighing a talent, over thirty kilograms (Exodus 25:31, 39). Three branches curved out on each side of a central stem, decorated with cups “made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower” (Exodus 25:33). It looked like a golden tree in blossom.

The oil was “pure beaten olive oil for the light” (Exodus 27:20), pressed gently from olives to burn clear with little smoke. The priests tended the lamps “from evening to morning before the LORD” (Exodus 27:21), trimming and refilling them each morning and lighting them each evening. With no windows, the lampstand was the room’s only light. Its small tools, “tongs and their trays” (Exodus 25:38), were wick-trimmers and dishes for the burnt ends, and they were made from the same talent of pure gold as the lampstand itself (Exodus 25:39).

The table and the bread of the Presence

Opposite, on the north side, stood a table of acacia wood overlaid with gold, about ninety centimetres long, forty-five wide and seventy high (Exodus 25:23). On it lay twelve large loaves, each made from “two tenths of an ephah” of fine flour (Leviticus 24:5), several litres each, in two piles of six with frankincense on each pile. Every Sabbath the priests set out fresh loaves and ate the old ones “in a holy place” (Leviticus 24:9). Its vessels were “plates and dishes for incense, and its flagons and bowls with which to pour drink offerings” (Exodus 25:29).

The Hebrew name means literally “bread of the face”, bread set before the face of God: twelve loaves for twelve tribes, “from the people of Israel as a covenant forever” (Leviticus 24:8). The whole people lived in God’s presence, fed by his provision. And because priests ate it in God’s house, it was a meal at his table, like the meal on Sinai when the elders “beheld God, and ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11).

The altar of incense

Straight ahead, before the great curtain, stood a small golden altar, about forty-five centimetres square and ninety high, with horns at its corners (Exodus 30:1–3). It was not for animals. “Every morning when he dresses the lamps he shall burn it, and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he shall burn it” (Exodus 30:7–8). Coals came from the bronze altar, so the fire of sacrifice lit the incense. God fixed the recipe, sweet spices with frankincense, “seasoned with salt, pure and holy” (Exodus 30:35), and no one was to copy it. When Nadab and Abihu offered “unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them” (Leviticus 10:1), they died. Worship is God’s to define. This altar belonged closely to the inner room, and Hebrews mentions it with the Most Holy Place (Hebrews 9:4). In Jesus’ day, while the priest burned incense, “the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense” (Luke 1:10).

Fulfilled in Christ

The light. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). Revelation names the lampstand directly. John sees “seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest” (Revelation 1:12–13), and he is told that “the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:20). That is level one. The churches are the lampstands, and the risen Christ, dressed like a priest, walks among them as the priests walked among the lamps, trimming and tending. Zechariah saw a lampstand fed with oil and heard, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). The church shines only with the oil of the Spirit.

The bread. Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). He said it of the manna, so linking it to the bread of the Presence is level two, but a fair one. Priests once ate holy bread at God’s table; now all believers, a priestly people, eat at the Lord’s Table, where “we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

The incense. Here the New Testament is plain. The elders in heaven hold “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5:8). David prayed, “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2). Level one: incense is prayer rising to God. In heaven an angel is given “much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints” (Revelation 8:3), as if something must be added to make them fragrant. Seeing in that the intercession of Christ is level two, but it fits what Hebrews says outright, that he “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25) for those who come to God through him. Our prayers are weak and mixed. They rise perfumed by his.

The spoons and the snuffers

And the small things: the tongs and trays, plates and dishes, flagons and bowls, and in Solomon’s temple the “cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans” (1 Kings 7:50)? This study will not invent a Christ-symbol for each. Scripture does not. But it does say three plain things about them.

They were made by God’s pattern, of the same pure gold as the great pieces. They were holy: when the camp moved they were wrapped in blue cloth and carried by Levites who must not touch them (Numbers 4:7–9, 15). When Belshazzar drank from the temple vessels at a drunken feast, judgment fell that night (Daniel 5:2–3, 30); when the exiles returned, Cyrus sent the vessels home, 5,400 of them, counted one by one (Ezra 1:7–11). God cared about his spoons. And they were for practical service: trimming wicks, carrying ash, pouring wine. The lesson is not hidden. Even the humblest work in God’s house is holy service.

Zechariah saw a day when that holiness would spread: “the pots in the house of the LORD shall be as the bowls before the altar. And every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy to the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 14:20–21). That day has dawned. In Christ the whole church is God’s temple, and every task done for him is holy. Washing cups after the service, setting out chairs, changing nappies in the crèche, running the sound desk: these are the wick-trimmers and ash pans of the new covenant, hidden from view, perhaps, but made of the same gold.

A retired man who had spent twenty years unlocking the church and stacking chairs once said he had never done anything for God. His minister read him Exodus 25:39 and Zechariah 14:20. The man was quiet for a while, and then said that he supposed the snuffers were gold too.

For reflection

What does the windowless Holy Place, lit only by the lampstand, teach about our need of Christ and his Spirit? How does it help you to know that your prayers rise to God joined to Christ’s intercession? What does God’s care for the smallest vessels say about the small tasks you do for him? Whose quiet, practical service in your church could you thank this week?

5.title: The Most Holy Place: The Ark and the Mercy Seat
5.essay:
Behind the great curtain lay a room no ordinary Israelite ever saw: dark, silent, and probably a perfect cube. It held one piece of furniture, a gold-covered chest with two golden figures bending over its lid. Here, God said, “I will meet with you” (Exodus 25:22). If the tabernacle was a sermon, this room was its climax.

The ark of the covenant

The ark was a chest of acacia wood two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide and high (Exodus 25:10), roughly 1.1 metres by 70 centimetres by 70, overlaid with pure gold inside and out. Two gold-covered poles ran through rings at its feet and were never to be removed (Exodus 25:15). It was carried on the Levites’ shoulders and never touched. When Uzzah put out his hand to steady it on a cart, “God struck him down there because of his error” (2 Samuel 6:7). Holiness is not a thing to handle casually.

Inside were the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, the “testimony” of God’s covenant (Exodus 25:16). With them, Hebrews tells us, were “a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded” (Hebrews 9:4). The manna recalled how God fed his people in the wilderness (Exodus 16:33–34). The staff recalled the rebellion of Korah and others against Aaron’s priesthood, settled when Aaron’s dry staff, overnight, “put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds” (Numbers 17:8). By Solomon’s day only the tablets remained (1 Kings 8:9).

The mercy seat and the cherubim

On the ark lay a lid of pure gold, the mercy seat. At each end, beaten from the same piece, stood a cherub, wings spread over the lid and face turned down towards it (Exodus 25:17–20). Cherubim in the Bible are mighty heavenly beings who guard God’s holiness, not chubby babies.

The Hebrew word for mercy seat, kapporet, comes from the word for atonement: it was the place where atonement was made. Israel spoke of God as “enthroned upon the cherubim” (Psalm 80:1), with the ark as his footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2). From there he spoke to Moses, “from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim” (Numbers 7:89). This was the throne room of Israel’s King, and his throne was a seat of mercy.

Think about what lay beneath that lid: the tablets of the law, which Israel broke almost as soon as they received it. Above the lid, the presence of the holy God. Between them, the mercy seat. And once a year the high priest sprinkled blood on it and before it (Leviticus 16:14–15). Unit 9, on the Day of Atonement, tells that day’s story. Seeing the blood as covering the broken law is level two, but it is how the arrangement works.

Who could go in

Almost no one. “Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat that is on the ark, so that he may not die” (Leviticus 16:2). Only the high priest, only on the Day of Atonement, only with blood and a cloud of incense. Hebrews sums it up: “into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood” (Hebrews 9:7). The curtain, a heavy veil of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen “with cherubim skillfully worked into it” (Exodus 26:31), guarded the way like the cherubim at the east of Eden. To every other Israelite it said: not yet, not you, not this way.

Fulfilled in Christ

Here the New Testament speaks at level one, again and again.

The mercy seat. Paul writes of Christ Jesus, “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25). The Greek word for “propitiation”, hilastērion, is the word the Greek Old Testament used for the mercy seat, and Hebrews 9:5 uses it in that sense. Propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin. Christ is the true mercy seat, where God’s holiness and our sin meet and blood makes peace. And notice who put him there: God himself, as he had provided the mercy seat. Israel did not invent it to calm an angry God. The tax collector in Jesus’ parable prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13), using a verb from the same family. In Christ that prayer is answered.

The curtain. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). From top to bottom: torn by God, not by man. Hebrews explains: we now “have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20). When his body was torn, the way into God’s presence was opened. What the high priest could do once a year, every believer may now do every day.

The high priest’s entry. Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12), and not into a tent room but “into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24).

Fair inferences. The manna in the ark points to Christ the bread from heaven, as Jesus said of the manna in John 6. Aaron’s dead staff that blossomed proved whom God had chosen as priest; it is fair to think of Christ, “declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). Some have noticed that Mary saw two angels “sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet” (John 20:12), like two cherubim over an empty mercy seat. John does not draw the link, so hold it lightly, as a devotional reflection. It is a beautiful one.

And the ark itself? It vanished, probably when Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC, and was never made again. Jeremiah had foreseen a day when “they shall no more say, ‘The ark of the covenant of the LORD.’ It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed” (Jeremiah 3:16). Why would no one miss it? Because something far better was coming.

What it means for us

Every believer now has what Israel’s high priest had one day a year, and more. “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). God’s throne is still a seat of mercy, and the way to it is open because of blood.

A woman raised to fear God but never told of the open curtain used to pray as though she stood outside a locked door. When she studied Hebrews 10 and saw that the curtain was torn from top to bottom, she wept. She was not sneaking in. She had been invited, by the blood of Christ, into the Most Holy Place.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that God’s throne in Israel was a mercy seat? Why does it matter that the curtain was torn from top to bottom? How should Hebrews 10:19–22 change the way you come to God in prayer? What did Israel have in the ark that you have far more fully in Christ?

6.title: From Tent to Temple
6.essay:
For nearly five hundred years God’s house was a tent. Then it became a building of stone, cedar and gold in Jerusalem. It was destroyed, rebuilt, enlarged and destroyed again. Why does a Christian need this history? Because the temple is one of the great threads that leads straight to Jesus, then to his people, and then to the end of all things.

David’s wish and God’s answer

Settled in his palace, David was troubled: “See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent” (2 Samuel 7:2). God turned the idea round. David would not build God a house; instead, “the LORD will make you a house” (2 Samuel 7:11), a dynasty. David’s son would build the temple, and God would “establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). From the start, the temple and the promised King belong together.

Solomon’s temple: glory and loss

Solomon built it on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1), where Abraham had once been told to offer Isaac. It followed the tabernacle’s plan at twice the size (1 Kings 6:2), with the Most Holy Place a cube of twenty cubits overlaid with gold. At the dedication the cloud of glory filled the house, “so that the priests could not stand to minister” (1 Kings 8:11). Yet Solomon prayed, “But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27). The temple was never a box for God. It was the place he chose to put his name, to hear prayer and to forgive.

Israel came to trust the building instead of the God who lived there. Jeremiah warned, “Do not trust in these deceptive words: ‘This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD’” (Jeremiah 7:4). Ezekiel saw the glory leave, and in 586 BC the Babylonians “burned the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 25:9). The study God with His People tells this sad part of the story.

The second temple and Herod’s temple

After the exile, under Zerubbabel, the returned exiles rebuilt the temple, finishing it in 516 BC (Ezra 6:15). Old men who remembered Solomon’s house “wept with a loud voice” (Ezra 3:12). But God promised, “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9), and “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1).

About 20 BC Herod the Great began rebuilding this second temple on a vast scale. It was still being worked on in Jesus’ day: “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple” (John 2:20). This is the temple of the Gospels. When his disciples admired its stones, Jesus said, “There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down” (Mark 13:2). In AD 70 the Romans burned it.

Something greater than the temple

Haggai’s promise came true, not through Herod’s marble, but because the Lord himself walked into that temple. Jesus said, “I tell you, something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6). When he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), John explains that “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21). That is level one. Jesus is the true temple: where God dwells in fullness, where heaven meets earth, where sinners meet God and find forgiveness. The place of worship is no longer a mountain but a person (John 4:21–23).

The church, God’s temple

Because believers are united to Christ, they too become God’s temple. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Jew and Gentile together are being built into “a holy temple in the Lord … a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21–22). This too is level one. The glory that filled the tabernacle now dwells, by the Spirit, in a people gathering each Lord’s Day in school halls, living rooms and chapels across the world.

The city with no temple

The thread ends in Revelation. The new Jerusalem is a cube, “its length and width and height are equal” (Revelation 21:16), like the Most Holy Place: the whole city has become the inner sanctuary. And John says, “I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). No building is needed when God is present to his people face to face.

Where Christians differ: Ezekiel’s temple

Ezekiel 40–48 describes a great temple in careful detail, with gates, courts, priests, sacrifices, and a river that turns the Dead Sea fresh (Ezekiel 47:1–9). Christians read it in different ways.

Many dispensational Christians expect a literal temple to be built in Jerusalem during a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth. Such precise measurements, they argue, would be strange if no building were meant. Some take its sacrifices as memorials looking back to the cross, as the Lord’s Supper does; others as offerings for ceremonial cleanness while sinners still live alongside the glorified King. They believe this takes God’s promises to Israel at face value.

Others, including most Reformed interpreters, read the vision as a picture painted in the language of Israel’s worship. It came “in visions of God” (Ezekiel 40:2), and its features point beyond any building: a river that grows deeper as it flows and gives life wherever it goes, the land divided into neat equal strips, and the city’s new name, “The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35).

This commentary’s view: the New Testament never expects a rebuilt temple or renewed sacrifice. Hebrews calls the old system “obsolete” and “ready to vanish away” (Hebrews 8:13), and Christ’s sacrifice was once for all. Ezekiel’s vision is fulfilled in Christ, the true temple; in his church, from which the living water of the Spirit flows (John 7:38–39); and finally in the new Jerusalem, where the river of the water of life flows “from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1). We hold this with respect for brothers and sisters who see it differently.

What it means for us

We need not travel to a holy place to meet God; we come through Christ, anywhere. But the local church is God’s temple now. A young man had drifted from church, thinking he could worship God just as well on a hillside. Then he read 1 Corinthians 3:16 and saw that Paul was speaking to a congregation, not a lone believer. God had chosen to live among a people, and he could not love the temple while staying away from its stones. He went back the next Sunday.

For reflection

Why do you think Israel came to trust the temple building rather than the God who lived there? What does it mean that Jesus is “something greater than the temple” (Matthew 12:6)? How should knowing that your church is God’s temple shape the way you treat other believers? What do you most look forward to in the city where there is no temple?

7.title: Priests, Levites and the High Priest
7.essay:
The idea of priesthood can seem strange or even suspicious: why should anyone stand between me and God? Yet the Old Testament gives page after page to Israel’s priests, their work and their clothes, because sinners need someone to stand between them and a holy God. The question is who.

The tribe of Levi

One of Israel’s twelve tribes, Levi, was set apart for the service of God’s house. When the people worshipped the golden calf, Moses stood in the gate of the camp and cried, “Who is on the LORD’s side? Come to me” (Exodus 32:26), and the sons of Levi rallied to him. Every family owed its firstborn son to the God who had spared them at the Passover, and God took the Levites “instead of every firstborn” (Numbers 3:12).

The Levites received no territory. God said, “I am your portion and your inheritance” (Numbers 18:20). They lived on the people’s tithes in forty-eight towns scattered through the tribes (Numbers 35:7), so that God’s word was never far from anyone. In the wilderness they dismantled, carried and set up the tabernacle (Numbers 4) and guarded the sanctuary. Later David organised them as gatekeepers, treasurers and musicians, “to stand every morning, thanking and praising the LORD” (1 Chronicles 23:30). Above all, they taught. After the exile they read the law “clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Bible World has more on priests and Levites.

The priests, sons of Aaron

Within Levi, only the descendants of Aaron were priests. They offered the sacrifices, burned the incense and tended the lamps. They blessed the people with the words God gave: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26). They judged between clean and unclean (see Unit 10), and they taught: “For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth” (Malachi 2:7). A priest was a go-between, bringing the people’s offerings to God and God’s word and blessing to the people.

The high priest and his garments

At their head stood the high priest. God designed his clothes “for glory and for beauty” (Exodus 28:2). Picture him.

Over a long linen tunic and sash came the robe, all of blue. Around its hem hung pomegranates of coloured yarn and little bells of gold, “a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate” (Exodus 28:34), so that when he served in the Holy Place the people outside could hear him (Exodus 28:35).

Over the robe came the ephod, a short apron-like garment of gold thread, coloured yarn and linen, with two shoulder straps. On each shoulder an onyx stone bore the names of six tribes, “stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel” (Exodus 28:12). Tied to the ephod across his chest was the breastpiece, a square pouch “a span its length and a span its breadth” (Exodus 28:16), about twenty-three centimetres, set with twelve precious stones in four rows, each engraved with a tribe’s name. “So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place” (Exodus 28:29).

Inside the breastpiece were the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:30), used to ask God for a decision (Numbers 27:21). We do not know exactly what they were or how they worked, and honest readers admit that Scripture tells us no more.

On his head was a linen turban, and on its front a plate of pure gold engraved “Holy to the LORD”, so that “Aaron shall bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate” (Exodus 28:38). Even Israel’s gifts to God were stained with sin, and the high priest’s holiness covered them.

Ordained, and failing

Aaron and his sons were ordained over seven days: washed, clothed, anointed and consecrated with sacrifices. Moses put blood on the right ear, the right thumb and the big toe of the right foot (Leviticus 8:23–24): all that they heard, did and walked towards belonged to God.

Yet the priesthood failed again and again. Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorised fire. The sons of Eli “treated the offering of the LORD with contempt” (1 Samuel 2:17). And the high priest Caiaphas presided over the trial of Jesus, saying, without knowing what he said, “it is better for you that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50). The high priest who should have carried the people on his heart handed the true High Priest over to death.

A priest like Melchizedek

Long before Aaron, Melchizedek, king of Salem and “priest of God Most High”, blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18). A thousand years later David wrote of his greater Son, “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Jesus was from Judah, not Levi, so he could not be a priest in Aaron’s line. Hebrews 7 explains that he is a priest of another order, appointed by God’s oath, king and priest in one, “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16).

Christ, the great High Priest

This is level one, the whole argument of Hebrews. Aaron’s priests died, but Christ “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:24–25). Aaron had to offer sacrifice for his own sins first; Christ had no sin, and “he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27). He is both priest and sacrifice, and he is not distant, for he “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

Now look again at the garments. Aaron carried the names of God’s people on his shoulders, the place of strength, and over his heart, the place of love, whenever he went in before God. Seeing Christ in this is level two, but it follows the grain of Hebrews: our High Priest has entered heaven “to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24). Your name is not lost in a crowd; he bears it before the Father. And “Holy to the LORD” describes perfectly the one Hebrews calls “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26), whose holiness covers even our best and most stained offerings.

A priesthood of all believers

Because Christ is our High Priest, every believer is a priest. Israel had been called “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:6), and Peter applies this to the church: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Every Christian may come straight to God, offer spiritual sacrifices (see Unit 8) and pray for others. We need no other human priest, for “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

That does not abolish ordered ministry. Christ gives shepherds and teachers “to equip the saints for the work of ministry” (Ephesians 4:12), and believers are to follow their leaders (Hebrews 13:17). But in this commentary’s understanding ministers are elders, not priests: they offer no sacrifices, but teach and shepherd a people who are all priests.

A nurse on night shifts felt she had little to give her church. An older friend told her she was a priest: on the wards she could carry the names of patients and colleagues before God, as Aaron carried Israel’s. She began to pray through her rota, name by name, and her work changed.

For reflection

Why do sinners need a priest at all? Which of the high priest’s garments helps you most to see Christ, and why? How does it comfort you that Jesus always lives to intercede for you? How could you use your priesthood as a believer this week, while honouring the leaders Christ has given your church?

8.title: The Five Offerings
8.essay:
Leviticus opens with seven chapters of bulls, rams, goats, pigeons, flour, oil, fat and blood, and many readers give up here. But picture an Israelite family walking to the tabernacle with an animal on a rope. They have sinned, or they are grateful, or they want to celebrate with God. Leviticus 1–7 tells them how: five offerings, five ways of coming to God, and every one fulfilled in Jesus.

Grace comes first

Leviticus begins, “The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting” (Leviticus 1:1). God had already rescued Israel and come to live among them. The sacrifices were not a way to earn his favour but his gift to a redeemed people. Timothy Keller often pointed out that religion runs on the principle, I obey, therefore I am accepted, while the gospel runs the other way: I am accepted through what God has done, therefore I obey. Leviticus comes after Exodus.

1. The burnt offering (Leviticus 1)

Brought: a male bull, ram or goat without blemish; for the poor, a dove or pigeon. Done: the worshipper laid his hand on its head, “and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him” (Leviticus 1:4). He killed it, the priests threw its blood against the altar, and the whole animal was burned. Eaten: nothing; only the skin went to the priest (Leviticus 7:8). Its name, ‘olah, means “what goes up”. Meaning: atonement, and complete devotion, nothing held back, “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9).

2. The grain offering (Leviticus 2)

Brought: fine flour with oil and frankincense, or loaves or wafers made from it, with no leaven or honey (Leviticus 2:11), but always salt, “the salt of the covenant with your God” (Leviticus 2:13). Done: the priest burned a handful with all the frankincense as a “memorial portion” (Leviticus 2:2). Eaten: the rest by the priests. Meaning: minchah means a gift or tribute. Flour is the fruit of ploughing, sowing, reaping and grinding, so this offering thanked God for his provision and gave him the work of one’s hands: first the self, in the burnt offering it usually accompanied, then the work.

3. The peace offering (Leviticus 3; 7:11–36)

Brought: a bull, sheep or goat, male or female, without blemish. Done: hand laid on it, blood thrown against the altar, the fat burned, for “all fat is the LORD’s” (Leviticus 3:16). Eaten: here is the surprise. The breast and right thigh went to the priests (Leviticus 7:31–32), and the worshipper’s family ate the rest in a joyful meal near God’s house. A thanksgiving offering had to be eaten the same day (Leviticus 7:15): joy is for sharing, not hoarding. Meaning: shelamim is related to shalom, peace and wholeness; some call it the fellowship offering. It was a meal with God, the sign of peace restored.

4. The sin offering (Leviticus 4:1–5:13)

Brought: it depended on who had sinned. For the high priest or the whole community, a bull; for a leader, a male goat; for an ordinary person, a female goat or lamb; for the poor, two birds; for the very poor, a little flour (Leviticus 5:7, 11). Done: the blood was put on the horns of the altar, and for the high priest or the community it was sprinkled inside, before the curtain. Eaten: for a leader or ordinary person, the priest ate the meat in a holy place (Leviticus 6:26); for the high priest or the community, the carcass was burned “outside the camp” (Leviticus 4:12). Meaning: chatta’t is often translated “purification offering”, because its blood cleansed the sanctuary as well as the sinner from sin’s defilement. It dealt especially with unintentional sins, noticed only later. The higher the office, the costlier the offering, because a leader’s sin harms many. And again and again comes the refrain: “and they shall be forgiven” (Leviticus 4:20).

When Mary brought the infant Jesus to the temple, she offered “a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24), the provision for a mother who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8). The poor family’s offering was brought for the child who would himself become the offering.

5. The guilt offering (Leviticus 5:14–6:7)

Brought: a ram without blemish, valued in silver shekels. Done: this was for wrongs that caused loss, misusing what belonged to God, or cheating a neighbour by fraud, theft or a false oath. The wrongdoer repaid in full “and shall add a fifth to it” (Leviticus 6:5), twenty per cent more, then brought the ram. Eaten: by the priests. Meaning: ‘asham is also called the reparation offering. Sin is a debt that does damage, and repentance includes putting things right, as Zacchaeus did when Jesus found him (Luke 19:8).

Christ, the fulfilment of all five

Hebrews hears Christ speaking in Psalm 40: “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me” (Hebrews 10:5). Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings, the whole range, give way to one obedient life offered on the cross: “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). That is level one.

He is our burnt offering, who held nothing back: he “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2), echoing Leviticus’ pleasing aroma. He is our grain offering, a whole life of perfect work offered to the Father, free of the leaven of sin (level two). He is our peace offering, “making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20), and at his Table we share in his sacrifice as Israel ate from theirs (1 Corinthians 10:16–18). He is our sin offering: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21), and like the sin offering burned outside the camp, “Jesus also suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12). He is our guilt offering: Isaiah foresaw the servant whose “soul makes an offering for guilt” (Isaiah 53:10). He paid a debt we could never repay, and gave back to God far more than we took.

Never enough, yet not useless

“For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). An animal cannot truly bear a person’s guilt, and the endless repetition showed the work was never finished: “in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year” (Hebrews 10:3).

Yet the sacrifices were not useless. God commanded them, and he really forgave those who brought them in faith. How, if animal blood could not remove sin? Paul answers that in his patience God “had passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25), forgiving believers in Israel on the strength of the sacrifice still to come. The offerings were like promissory notes, honoured in full at the cross. Meanwhile they taught Israel that sin is deadly, God is holy, and a substitute can die in the sinner’s place. They were never meant to work without faith and repentance. The prophets condemned those who brought animals while living in sin (Isaiah 1:11; Hosea 6:6), and David knew that “the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psalm 51:17).

Our offerings now

Christ’s offering is complete. But believers still offer sacrifices, not to win forgiveness but in thanks for it. “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1): that is the burnt offering, all of us given to God. “Let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15): the thanksgiving of the peace offering. Doing good and sharing what we have are “sacrifices … pleasing to God” (Hebrews 13:16): the grain offering’s work and gifts. And the guilt offering still teaches us to make things right with those we have wronged (Matthew 5:23–24).

A businessman converted in his fifties remembered underpaying a supplier years before. He knew he could add nothing to Christ’s forgiveness, but after reading Leviticus 6 he repaid the money and added a fifth. The supplier rang to ask why, and it became the most natural conversation about Jesus he had ever had.

For reflection

Which of the five offerings helps you most to understand what Christ has done for you? What difference does it make that the sacrifices were given to a people already redeemed? How could the sacrifices truly bring forgiveness if animal blood could not take away sin? Which spiritual sacrifice is God calling you to offer this week?

9.title: The Day of Atonement
9.essay:
Picture the camp of Israel on the tenth day of the seventh month. Nobody is working or eating. The nation waits in silence while one man goes where no one else may go, carrying blood. This was the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day of Israel’s year, and the letter to the Hebrews says it was a rehearsal for Jesus.

A day that began with a grave

Leviticus 16 is dated by a funeral: God spoke “after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD and died” (Leviticus 16:1). Two priests had come near in their own way and been consumed (Leviticus 10:1–2). So Aaron must not come “at any time” behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place, where the ark and the mercy seat stood (Unit 5 describes them), “so that he may not die” (Leviticus 16:2). Yet the next words are pure grace: “But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place” (Leviticus 16:3). There is a way in, and God describes it.

What happened that day

Plain clothes. On other days the high priest wore gold, blue, purple and scarlet, with twelve jewels on his chest (Unit 7). Today he bathed and put on “the holy linen coat” (Leviticus 16:4): on the greatest day of the year he dressed like a servant.

A bull for himself. Before dealing with anyone else’s sin he had to “make atonement for himself and for his house” (Leviticus 16:6). The mediator came as a sinner first.

Incense and blood. Hidden in a cloud of incense, “so that he does not die”, he sprinkled the bull’s blood on the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:13–14).

Two goats. Lots were cast over two goats. One was killed as a sin offering for the people, and its blood too was taken inside. Afterwards the carcasses whose blood had gone inside were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), while the people fasted, did no work and humbled themselves before God (Leviticus 16:29). All of this happened “once in the year” (Leviticus 16:34).

Two goats, one atonement

Why two goats? Because sin is two problems at once. It deserves God’s just judgment, and it clings to us and defiles. The first goat died, and its blood on the mercy seat showed that a life had been given in the sinners’ place, so that God’s just anger was turned away. Over the second goat Aaron was to “confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins” (Leviticus 16:21). Then a man led it into the desert: “The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area” (Leviticus 16:22). Israel watched their sins walk away and not come back.

The goat was sent “to Azazel”, a word no one is sure of. Later Jewish tradition made it a desert demon; this commentary thinks it most likely means the barren wilderness itself, cut off from God’s camp. Either way, the goat was sent, not sacrificed to anyone. (Our word “scapegoat” comes from Tyndale’s translation of 1530.) David sang what that walk meant: “as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).

What Hebrews sees

Here we are on firm ground, because the New Testament itself names the fulfilment. Into the inner room “only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people” (Hebrews 9:7). The way in was “not yet opened” (Hebrews 9:8). Then Hebrews sets Jesus beside Aaron.

Aaron needed a sacrifice for himself; Jesus is “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26). Aaron brought animal blood; Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). Aaron came back every year; Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). The old priests stood; Christ “sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). And the bodies burned outside the camp find their answer too: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

The New Testament never names the goat that was sent away, so here we move from what is named to what is consistent with the New Testament, a fair inference from what it does say: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), and Jesus is “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Christ is both the one who died and the one who carried our sins away.

When the priest came out

When Israel saw the high priest step out alive, they knew the sacrifice had been accepted. Hebrews seems to have that waiting crowd in mind when it says that Christ “will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him” (Hebrews 9:28).

A woman in her sixties had confessed the same sin from her twenties every night for forty years. Reading Leviticus 16 with her pastor, she noticed that the old sacrifices brought “a reminder of sins every year” (Hebrews 10:3), but that in the new covenant God says, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more” (Hebrews 10:17). She said it was like watching the goat disappear over the horizon. That night she thanked God instead.

Jewish people still keep Yom Kippur with fasting and prayer (the study Christ in the Old Testament describes it). But the Christian has no annual day of dread. The curtain is torn. “Since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus … let us draw near” (Hebrews 10:19–22). What one man did once a year in fear, every believer may now do every day, because the true High Priest went in with his own blood, and came out of the tomb alive.

For reflection

Why did the Day of Atonement need two goats? Which contrast between Aaron and Christ in Hebrews 9–10 means most to you? Is there a sin you keep confessing as if it had never been carried away? How would you explain to a friend why Christians need no yearly day of atonement?

10.title: Clean and Unclean, and the Food Laws
10.essay:
Why could an Israelite eat a sheep but not a pig, a cod but not a prawn? Why did burying your father make you “unclean” for a week? Leviticus 11 to 15 can look like a strange mix of menu, medicine and superstition. But these chapters teach something deep about God, about life and death, and about Jesus, who touched the untouchable.

Holy, common, clean, unclean

God told the priests: “You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean” (Leviticus 10:10). Picture four zones. Holy things belonged to God: the tabernacle, the priests, the offerings. Everything else was common, that is, ordinary. Common things could be clean, the normal state, or unclean, unfit for a time to come near God’s sanctuary.

Unclean did not mean sinful. A mother after childbirth was unclean (Leviticus 12:2). So was a son who buried his father: “Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days” (Numbers 19:11). Uncleanness was a ritual state, dealt with by waiting, washing and sometimes an offering, before you came near the holy God.

Why these things?

Look at what made people unclean: corpses, skin disease that made the living body look as if it were decaying, and the loss of blood and other fluids tied to life. Many scholars see a common thread: death, or the signs of it. God is the living God, and death had no place in his presence. The law gives its own reason: “lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst” (Leviticus 15:31).

Skin disease is the clearest picture. (The Hebrew word covered several conditions, not only what we call leprosy.) The sufferer had to “cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean.’ … He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:45–46). The priest could examine, but he could not heal.

The food lists

Land animals had to have a split hoof and chew the cud, like cattle, sheep and goats (Leviticus 11:3), so the pig was out (Leviticus 11:7). Water creatures needed “fins and scales” (Leviticus 11:9), so no shellfish.

Why? The text never explains each rule, and readers have offered several reasons. Some point to health: pork and shellfish can carry disease in a hot climate. That may be a side benefit, but it hardly explains every rule. Some point to pagan practices, which fits a few laws, such as not boiling a young goat in its mother’s milk (Exodus 23:19), but not most. Some see a symbolic order: clean animals fit neatly into their kind, a lesson in wholeness. Others see death and life again, since many forbidden creatures eat carrion or flesh. This commentary thinks that last thread is the clearest, but holds it humbly.

What is certain is the reason the text does give: “be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). The menu marked Israel out: “I am the LORD your God, who has separated you from the peoples. You shall therefore separate the clean beast from the unclean” (Leviticus 20:24–25). An Israelite could not eat lunch without remembering whose he was.

The Lord who touched the unclean

Now watch Jesus. A leper knelt before him, and “Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, ‘I will; be clean’” (Mark 1:41). By the law, touching a leper made you unclean. But the uncleanness did not flow into Jesus; cleanness flowed into the leper. A woman with twelve years of bleeding touched his garment and was healed (Mark 5:27–29). He took a dead girl by the hand (Mark 5:41). Every great source of uncleanness met him, and every one gave way. Here is a fair inference, consistent with the New Testament: the purity laws were a long lesson in how far death had spread, and Jesus came as the life that death could not defile.

Then he moved the line to where it had always pointed: “There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him” (Mark 7:15). Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Peter learned it on a rooftop in Joppa, “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Acts 10:15), and soon saw it was about people too: “God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean” (Acts 10:28). The food laws had kept Jew and Gentile at separate tables. In Christ they eat together, for “the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

Where Christians differ

Seventh-day Adventists keep the Leviticus 11 distinctions as God’s guidance for health, never withdrawn. Some Messianic Jewish believers keep a kosher diet as part of their Jewish calling, not as a way of being saved. Both deserve a respectful hearing.

This commentary’s view: all foods are clean for the Christian (Mark 7:19; Acts 10; 1 Timothy 4:4). The rules of Acts 15 served table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers at that time. Jewish believers are free to keep the old customs as devotion, but never as the way of salvation or a test of fellowship: “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains” (Romans 14:3).

What remains: a clean heart

The menu changed; the reason for it did not. Peter quotes Leviticus: “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15). And what no washing could reach, Christ reaches: “how much more will the blood of Christ … purify our conscience” (Hebrews 9:14).

A woman abused as a teenager told her pastor she had felt dirty ever since, though the sin was not hers. They read Mark 1 together, and she saw that Jesus did not keep his distance from the leper: he reached out first. Over many months, with a good counsellor and her church beside her, she began to believe that his touch makes clean what others made unclean. (If you have been abused, your safety comes first: tell someone you trust and report it to the police, today if it is still happening.)

Leviticus shows how seriously God takes defilement. Jesus shows how far he came to remove it: to the cross outside the city, where he bore our sin so that we might be clean for ever.

For reflection

Why does it matter that “unclean” in Leviticus did not simply mean “sinful”? Which explanation of the food laws do you find most convincing? What does it tell you about Jesus that he touched the leper before healing him? Where do you need his cleansing today?

11.title: The Feasts: Passover to Pentecost
11.essay:
Israel’s year was shaped by feasts. Three times a year every man went up to worship (Deuteronomy 16:16). God called them “the appointed feasts of the LORD” (Leviticus 23:2): not holidays Israel invented, but meetings God put in the diary. The spring feasts are some of the clearest pictures of Christ in the whole Old Testament, because he kept them, died at one, rose at another, and poured out his Spirit at a third.

Passover: the night of the blood

Passover remembered the night God set Israel free from Egypt. Each household took a lamb, “without blemish, a male a year old” (Exodus 12:5), and kept it in the house for four days. At twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month they killed it, painted its blood on the doorposts and the beam above the door with a bunch of hyssop, and ate it roasted, “with unleavened bread and bitter herbs” (Exodus 12:8). They ate dressed for a journey, “in haste” (Exodus 12:11). That night the firstborn of Egypt died, but God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13).

Passover was a meal of memory, and it was built to be explained. God expected children to ask, “What do you mean by this service?” and the answer was: “It is the sacrifice of the LORD’s Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt” (Exodus 12:26–27).

Christ our Passover

This is firm ground; the New Testament names it. Paul writes, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Jesus died at Passover time, and John notices that, as with the Passover lamb, none of his bones was broken: “Not one of his bones will be broken” (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46).

And on the night before he died, Jesus sat down to a Passover meal with his disciples. “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). Then he took the bread of the meal and said, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And he took the cup: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:19–20). The meal that remembered the lamb in Egypt became the meal that remembers the Lamb of God. The Lord’s Supper is not a Passover Seder, but it grew out of one, and it answers the same question the children asked: what does this mean? It means a death in our place, and blood that turns judgment away.

Unleavened Bread: leaving in a hurry

Passover led straight into a seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread. Leaven was a lump of old, fermented dough kept back to make the next batch rise. For a week, every scrap was cleared out of the house. The bread was flat because Israel left Egypt with no time to let it rise (Exodus 12:39). Moses called it “the bread of affliction”, eaten “that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 16:3).

Paul draws the lesson himself: “Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened.” Because “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed”, we are to “celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:7–8). Israel did not clean the house in order to be rescued. They were rescued, and so they cleaned the house. So do we: we clear out the old sour dough of sin because the Lamb has already died.

Firstfruits: the first sheaf

In the same week, when the barley harvest began, a farmer brought “the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest”, who waved it before the LORD “on the day after the Sabbath” (Leviticus 23:10–11). Nobody ate the new crop until the first sheaf had been given to God (Leviticus 23:14). It was a thank-you and a pledge: more is coming.

Paul names the fulfilment: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Jesus rose on the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath of Passover week. His resurrection is the first sheaf of a vast harvest: “Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:23). Every Christian grave is a field waiting for harvest.

Weeks: the harvest and the Spirit

Israel then counted seven weeks, “fifty days”, to the next feast (Leviticus 23:16). The Greek word for fiftieth gives us its other name, Pentecost. It was the wheat-harvest festival: two loaves of the new grain were waved before the LORD (Leviticus 23:17), and everyone was to rejoice, “you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite … the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow” (Deuteronomy 16:11). Later Jewish tradition linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai, though the Old Testament does not.

Then, fifty days after the resurrection, “When the day of Pentecost arrived” (Acts 2:1), the Holy Spirit came. Pilgrims were in Jerusalem “from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5), and that day about three thousand were added to the church (Acts 2:41). The timing is named in the New Testament; its meaning is a fair inference that Paul’s language supports, for he calls the Spirit “the firstfruits” (Romans 8:23). The harvest feast became the first great harvest of the nations.

Some have noticed that about three thousand died at Sinai after the golden calf (Exodus 32:28) and about three thousand were saved at Pentecost; others see Jew and Gentile in the two loaves. Such reflections may warm the heart, but hold them lightly: the New Testament does not draw them, and they are not doctrine.

One spring, one gospel

Look at the spring calendar: a lamb slain, a house cleaned out, a first sheaf lifted up, a harvest fifty days later. Then look at the first Easter: Christ crucified at Passover, raised on the day after the Sabbath, the Spirit poured out at Pentecost. God wrote the dates of the gospel into Israel’s farming year more than a thousand years before. No clever reader invented that pattern. It is the hand of the God who rules history.

A young Christian was invited to a Jewish friend’s Passover meal. She listened as the youngest child asked why this night is different from all other nights, and as the family told of the lamb and the blood. On the way home she wept. The next Sunday, when her church took the Lord’s Supper, she heard “This is my body, which is given for you” as if for the first time.

For reflection

What does Passover teach about how God saves: by our goodness, or by the blood of a substitute? Why does Paul put the cleaning out of the old leaven after Christ’s sacrifice, not before it? How does knowing that Christ is “the firstfruits” change the way you think about death? What does Pentecost, the harvest feast, suggest about the church’s mission to the nations?

12.title: The Autumn Feasts, the Sabbath and the Jubilee
12.essay:
The autumn feasts, the weekly Sabbath, the seventh year and the fiftieth all taught Israel that time belongs to God. Some of these pictures were fulfilled when Christ first came. Others are still pointing forward, like a signpost to a city we have not yet reached.

Trumpets

The seventh month opened with “a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation” (Leviticus 23:24). Trumpets called Israel together and marked the start of each month (Numbers 10:10). The Feast of Trumpets woke Israel up for the most solemn month of the year. Later Jewish tradition made it the New Year, Rosh Hashanah, a time for self-examination.

The New Testament never names the Feast of Trumpets as fulfilled. But it does speak of a trumpet still to sound: Christ will come “with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), “at the last trumpet” (1 Corinthians 15:52). To see the autumn feasts as a picture of what is still ahead is a fair inference. To build a timetable for the second coming from the Jewish calendar goes beyond Scripture.

The Day of Atonement
