Ten days later came the Day of Atonement, which Unit 9 describes: the high priest behind the curtain, the two goats, and Christ who entered once for all with his own blood.

Booths: camping with God

Five days after that came the happiest week of the year, the Feast of Booths, also called Tabernacles. The harvest was in. Families cut “branches of palm trees and boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook” and built rough shelters, and for seven days they lived in them: “that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:40–43). Imagine a whole nation camping out, remembering the wilderness years when God lived among them in his own tent. Deuteronomy says the point was joy: “you will be altogether joyful” (Deuteronomy 16:15).

By Jesus’ day, Jewish sources tell us, two ceremonies had been added at the temple: each morning a priest poured water from the Pool of Siloam beside the altar, and at night huge lamps lit up the temple courts. Now read John 7 and 8. It was the Feast of Booths (John 7:2). “On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’”, and John explains that he meant the Spirit (John 7:37–39). Soon after he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Against the water and the lights of Booths, Jesus was saying: this feast is about me.

John had already used the feast’s own language when he wrote that the Word “dwelt” among us, literally pitched his tent (Unit 2 explains this). Its final fulfilment is the new creation: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). There a great multitude stands before the Lamb “with palm branches in their hands” (Revelation 7:9). The camping is over. We are home.

The Sabbath

Every seventh day Israel stopped. The Sabbath was rooted in creation: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth … and rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11). It was also rooted in redemption: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves never get a day off; God’s freed people did, and so did their own servants. God called it “a sign between me and you” (Exodus 31:13).

Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). He offered the rest it pictured: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Hebrews says “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), entered by trusting Christ and completed in glory. Paul calls the Sabbath, with the festivals, “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). All this is named in the New Testament.

Christians differ on what this means for Sunday. Many godly Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Baptist Confessions, hold that the fourth commandment is moral and permanent, so that Sunday is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept by rest from ordinary work and recreation. Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. Others hold that the Sabbath was the sign of the Mosaic covenant and is fulfilled in Christ.

This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day, the first day, the day of resurrection (Revelation 1:10), is his gift. It should be gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, and gathering with God’s people must not be neglected (Hebrews 10:25). But it is not a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience: “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). Here this commentary differs from the 1689 Confession it otherwise follows. The study Worship & the Lord’s Day sets out the question more fully.

The seventh year and the fiftieth

The Sabbath pattern stretched across years. Every seventh year the land rested: “You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard” (Leviticus 25:4), and debts between Israelites were released (Deuteronomy 15:1–2). That was the sabbath year. After seven times seven years, on the Day of Atonement, the trumpet sounded across the land to begin the Jubilee: “proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants … each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan” (Leviticus 25:9–10). Israelites who had sold themselves into service went free, and family land that had been sold went back to its family. The reason: “the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). No poverty was meant to be permanent, because everything belonged to God.

Israel seems seldom to have kept it (2 Chronicles 36:21). But one Sabbath in Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah 61: “He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives … to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” Then he sat down and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:18–21). That is named in the New Testament. The Jubilee trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, and our liberty is bought by the blood of the cross: debts cancelled, slaves freed, the lost inheritance given back.

A nurse working long shifts used to treat Sunday as catch-up day. When she began to keep it as a gift, with worship in the morning and her phone switched off in the afternoon, she found she was not falling behind; she was learning to trust. Every week reminded her that the world does not depend on her, and that a greater rest is coming.

For reflection

Why do you think God built celebration and rest into Israel’s calendar, not only work and sacrifice? What does Jesus’ cry at the Feast of Booths offer you today? How can Christians who differ on the Sabbath honour one another? Which part of the Jubilee (cancelled debt, freedom, or a restored inheritance) do you most need to hear as good news?

13.title: The Law and the Christian
13.essay:
A colleague once waved a phone at a Christian in the office: “Leviticus says you can’t wear mixed fabrics. Is your shirt a sin?” It is a fair question, and many believers do not know how to answer it. Which of the Old Testament’s laws still apply, and how? The answer begins not with a list but with a rescue.

Rescue first, then law

God did not give Israel the law in Egypt as a test to pass before he would save them. He gave it at Sinai, after the Red Sea. His first words were: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Before that he had said, “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4). The law was the shape of life for a people already redeemed.

So the law was a gift, given “for our good always” (Deuteronomy 6:24). The psalmist sang, “The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7). The study The Ten Commandments explores this at length, including the three uses of the law that Calvin taught: it shows us our sin, restrains evil in society, and guides believers in grateful living. This unit asks the wider question: what about the other six hundred or so commands?

Moral, civil and ceremonial

The Reformed tradition has long sorted the laws of Moses into three kinds. The Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession, in their chapters on the law, put it like this. Ceremonial laws (sacrifices, priesthood, festivals, food and purity laws) were pictures of Christ and are now fulfilled and ended. Civil or judicial laws governed Israel as a nation under God; they expired with that nation, though their “general equity”, the justice they express, still teaches us. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflects God’s own character and binds everyone always.

This distinction has real strengths. The New Testament itself treats the sacrifices and food laws as finished (Hebrews 8:13; Mark 7:19), while it repeats moral commands as still binding: “Honor your father and mother” (Ephesians 6:2). And it helps ordinary Christians neither throw the Old Testament away nor try to keep it all.

It also has limits, and it is honest to say so. Israel never labelled its laws this way. A single chapter can mix all three: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” sits one verse away from “nor shall you wear a garment of cloth made of two kinds of material” (Leviticus 19:18–19). Some laws are hard to sort; the Sabbath is both one of the Ten and a ceremonial sign. And Paul treats the law of Moses as one package: whoever takes it up as the way to be right with God “is obligated to keep the whole law” (Galatians 5:3). So the threefold distinction is best used as a helpful map, not a set of watertight boxes. The deeper truth is that the whole law comes to us through Christ.

Christ fulfils the law

Jesus said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). He kept every command perfectly in our place. He was the sacrifice the ceremonial laws pictured, and the King whose kingdom the civil laws foreshadowed. Paul says “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4): the end as the goal it aimed at, and the end of it as a way to earn God’s favour. The law was “our guardian until Christ came” (Galatians 3:24), like the household slave who walked a child to school.

And he writes it on our hearts. God promised, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Christians are not lawless; Paul says he is “under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21), and love is its heart: “love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:10).

Where Christians differ

Reformed covenant theology holds the threefold distinction above, with the Ten Commandments as the permanent moral law. Theonomy, a minority Reformed view, holds that Israel’s civil laws, including their penalties, should guide modern governments unless the New Testament changes them, because God’s justice does not change. New Covenant Theology holds that the whole Mosaic covenant, Ten Commandments included, has ended as a covenant, and that Christians are under the law of Christ, which takes up the moral commands the New Testament repeats. Dispensational teachers see the law of Moses as the rule for Israel in a dispensation now closed; the church lives under grace and the law of Christ, though the moral principles of the old law are still instructive. Each view wants to honour both Testaments.

This commentary’s view: with the 1689 Confession, Israel’s civil and ceremonial laws are fulfilled and ended, and the moral law remains the rule of life for believers. It is the shape of love, never a way to earn salvation. Theonomy, in this commentary’s judgment, overlooks how much changed when God’s people ceased to be a single nation with a land and became a church from every nation. (On the one point where this commentary sees the Sabbath differently from the Confession, see Unit 12.)

How to read a law today

Take any law and ask three questions. What does it show about God? What does it show about sin and about us? How is it fulfilled in Christ and applied through love?

Here is a law that might look irrelevant: “When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it” (Deuteronomy 22:8). Israelites used flat roofs as living space. God cares about human life, even in building regulations. Carelessness that endangers others is sin. Christ fulfils it as the neighbour who did more than build a wall: he laid down his life to keep us from falling. And love today puts a fence round the swimming pool, keeps the workplace safe and drives with care.

Paul does exactly this with another law: “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” He asks, “Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake?” (1 Corinthians 9:9–10). The ox law teaches that workers, including gospel workers, should share in what their work produces.

And the mixed fabrics? Like the food laws, they were part of a visible system of separation that taught Israel to keep things distinct and to be a distinct people (Unit 10). Christ has fulfilled that sign. The lesson behind it, an undivided life given to God, remains. The Christian in the office needn’t check the label on his shirt. But he can answer with joy: the law was a gift for a rescued people, it is fulfilled in Jesus, and what it was always about, loving God and neighbour, is now written on his heart.

For reflection

Why does it matter that God rescued Israel before he gave the law? What are the strengths and the limits of the threefold division of the law? Choose a law from Leviticus or Deuteronomy and ask the three questions of it. How does the gospel free you to love God’s law rather than fear it?

14.title: The Hard Laws
14.essay:
Some Old Testament laws trouble Christians, and they should. There are laws about slaves, commands to destroy whole cities, death penalties for adultery and Sabbath-breaking, and laws about women that sound harsh to modern ears. Sceptics read them aloud to show that the Bible is cruel. This unit does not hurry past them. It asks what they actually say, what they meant in their world, where they lead, and what remains hard.

Slavery and debt servitude

Most “slavery” among Israelites was debt servitude. A man who could not pay his debts sold his labour, and the law limited it: “he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing” (Exodus 21:2). He was not to be sent away “empty-handed”, but given a generous start, because “you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (Deuteronomy 15:13–15). Leviticus adds: “You shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:43).

Compared with the ancient Near East, some of these laws are startling. The Code of Hammurabi made it a capital crime to help a runaway slave escape. Israel’s law said: “You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you” (Deuteronomy 23:15). A slave who lost an eye or a tooth from his master’s blow went free (Exodus 21:26–27). Kidnapping a person to sell him was punishable by death (Exodus 21:16), which condemns the very trade that filled the Atlantic slave ships, and Paul lists “enslavers” among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10).

Honesty requires more. Foreign slaves could be held for life and passed on as property (Leviticus 25:44–46), and one law says of a slave beaten who survives that “the slave is his money” (Exodus 21:21). The law of Moses regulated a fallen practice in a fallen world; it did not create it, and it did not abolish it. Jesus explained one such law in a way that helps here: Moses allowed divorce “Because of your hardness of heart … but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). Some laws restrain evil rather than describe the ideal. And the direction of Scripture runs one way: Job asked of his servant, “Did not he who made me in the womb make him?” (Job 31:15), and Paul sent Onesimus back “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). That seed grew, slowly, into Christian abolitionism. (See Slavery in the Ancient World.)

The conquest of Canaan

God commanded Israel to devote the Canaanite cities to destruction, the Hebrew word herem, meaning something handed over wholly to God. Joshua 6 says plainly that at Jericho this included the young and the old. This commentary’s notes on Joshua 6 do not soften that, and neither should we.

But we must also hear what the Bible puts around it. First, the judgment was long delayed. God told Abraham his descendants would wait four generations, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). The Canaanites were not innocent; Scripture names the reason again and again: “they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods” (Deuteronomy 12:31). Second, it was not about Israel’s goodness: “Not because of your righteousness … but because of the wickedness of these nations” (Deuteronomy 9:5). Israel was warned that the land would “vomit you out” too if they did the same (Leviticus 18:28), and centuries later it did. Third, it was never about race. Rahab, a Canaanite, believed, and her household was spared and grafted into the line of the Messiah. Fourth, it was a unique, limited command, never a pattern. No prophet or apostle repeats it, and the Christian’s weapons “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Some scholars add that ancient war reports used sweeping language: Joshua 10:40 says Joshua “left none remaining”, yet Judges 1 shows many Canaanites still in the land. The scale may have been smaller than it first appears, but that does not remove the hard core, and we should not pretend it does. In the end we stand with Abraham: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25), and with the God who says, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11).

The death penalty in Israel

Israel’s law prescribed death for murder, but also for adultery (Leviticus 20:10), striking or cursing a parent (Exodus 21:15, 17), idolatry (Deuteronomy 13:6–10) and Sabbath-breaking (Numbers 15:32–36). Several things help. Israel was a unique nation with God living in its midst; its sins were treason against its King, in his own camp. The law demanded careful evidence: “a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness” (Deuteronomy 17:6). Some scholars note that only for murder is a ransom forbidden (Numbers 35:31), which may mean lesser penalties were often accepted for other crimes.

And see how the New Testament carries these laws over. When a man in Corinth was living in gross sin, Paul quoted Deuteronomy: “Purge the evil person from among you” (1 Corinthians 5:13). But the church did not stone him; it removed him from fellowship, hoping for his repentance. The holiness is the same; the means has changed, because God’s people are no longer a nation-state. The death penalty for murder, however, rests on something older than Moses: “for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). This commentary holds that the state may still punish murder with death, justly and with great care.

Women in the law

Some laws reflect a world where women had little power. The law did not abolish that world, but it often worked against its cruelty. A woman attacked “in the open country” was presumed innocent, because “there was no one to rescue her” (Deuteronomy 22:27). A neglected wife could go free (Exodus 21:10–11). The daughters of Zelophehad asked for their father’s land, and God said, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right” (Numbers 27:7). Other laws remain hard to read, such as the rules for a captive woman (Deuteronomy 21:10–14), though even there she could not be sold or treated as a slave. And the trajectory is again clear: Jesus welcomed, taught and honoured women, and in Christ “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

Living with what is hard

A student’s atheist friend read Deuteronomy 20 to her over coffee. She had no quick answer, and said so. A week later, having read the chapters around it, she told him what she had found, admitted what still troubled her, and added: the God of these chapters did not stand at a distance from judgment. In the end he stepped into it himself.

That is where every hard law finally leads. Our outrage at the death of the young and the weak comes from the Bible’s own conviction that every person bears God’s image. And Scripture answers that outrage at the cross, where “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). There God showed himself both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The Judge of all the earth did right, and then took the judgment on himself. For the wider questions of evil and suffering, see the study Apologetics, Unit 3.

For reflection

Which of these hard laws troubles you most, and why? How does Jesus’ comment on divorce (Matthew 19:8) help us read laws that regulate rather than approve? What does the story of Rahab show about the conquest? How does the cross change the way you hold questions you cannot yet answer?

15.title: Reading the Stories Well
15.essay:
Most of the Old Testament is story: families, wars, kings, journeys, scandals. Many of us were taught these stories as children, with a moral at the end: be brave like David, be faithful like Daniel, don’t be greedy like Achan. There is truth in that, but it misses the main thing. The Old Testament stories are not mainly about heroes to copy. They are about God, and they are heading for Christ.

Describing is not approving

The first rule is simple: the Bible often describes what it does not approve. Abraham passed his wife off as his sister, twice. Jacob cheated his brother. Jephthah made a rash vow and kept it at a terrible cost. Judges ends its darkest chapters with a verdict: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). The narrator often lets the facts speak and trusts us to see the wrong. A story is not a command. To know whether an action is commended we look at the whole story, at what God says and does in it, and at the rest of Scripture.

The heroes are flawed; God is the hero

Almost every great figure in the Old Testament fails. Noah gets drunk. Moses loses his temper and is barred from the land. David, the man after God’s own heart, commits adultery and arranges a murder. Solomon, the wisest man of his age, is led astray by his wives. If these stories were mainly about role models, they would be strangely discouraging.

But they are not mainly about the people. They are about the God who keeps his promises through people like this. Joseph says to the brothers who sold him: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive” (Genesis 50:20). Hebrews 11 commends the faith of Gideon, Samson and Jephthah, not because they were admirable men, but because a weak faith in a great God is still faith. Ask of every story, “What is God doing here?” before you ask, “What should I do?”

Read the whole story

The Old Testament is not a collection of separate tales. It is one long story with threads running through it. In the garden God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). He promised Abraham that “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). He promised David a son whose throne would last “forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). Each story moves those promises forward, or seems to put them in danger. Will the line of promise survive a barren wife, a famine, a murderous king? The tension is the point. The study The Big Story of the Bible traces these threads from Eden to the new Jerusalem. Then the New Testament says: “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

The true and better

Timothy Keller often pointed out that each great figure of the Old Testament is a sketch of someone greater, and that Jesus is the true and better version of each. He meant something like this.

Adam was tested in a garden and fell, and we fell with him. Jesus is the true and better Adam, tested in a wilderness and then in another garden, and he did not fall. Paul calls Adam “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14). Abraham left his home and his father’s house at God’s call, not knowing where he was going. Jesus left the glory of his Father’s house to come to us. Isaac carried the wood up the mountain, and Abraham said, “God will provide for himself the lamb” (Genesis 22:8). Isaac was spared at the last moment; Jesus carried his cross up the hill and was not spared: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

Joseph was betrayed by his brothers, sold, and then raised to the right hand of the king, from where he forgave and fed the very men who had betrayed him. Moses stood between the people and God and led them out of slavery, but Jesus “has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses” (Hebrews 3:3). David faced the giant when all Israel was terrified. Jonah was thrown into the sea so that the storm would stop and the sailors would live (Jonah 1:12); Jesus spoke of “the sign of the prophet Jonah” and said, “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:39–41).

Some of these links are named in the New Testament: Adam, Moses, Jonah, David. Others, such as Joseph and the binding of Isaac, are fair inferences that fit the New Testament’s own pattern (Hebrews 11:19 even says Abraham received Isaac back “figuratively speaking” from the dead). Notice that the comparisons work because the stories are real history, not because we have hunted for hidden codes in them.

Not “be like David”

Take David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17). The usual lesson is: be brave like David, and your giants will fall. But read the story whole. Goliath proposed a contest between two champions, each fighting for his whole people: whoever lost, his people would serve the other side (1 Samuel 17:9). And “Saul and all Israel … were dismayed and greatly afraid” (1 Samuel 17:11). Where are we in this story? Not in David’s sandals. We are with the trembling Israelites in the valley. David, the newly anointed king, went out alone as Israel’s representative, and his victory became theirs, so that the army that had done nothing chased the Philistines and plundered their camp.

So the gospel reading of the story is not “be brave like David” but “Christ is the greater David who fought for us.” He went out alone against sin, death and the devil, and won, and his victory becomes ours: through death he destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Then, and only then, comes courage. Those who have been rescued by the champion can face their own battles, because “the battle is the LORD’s” (1 Samuel 17:47).

That does not mean the stories have no moral lessons. Paul says the wilderness stories “happened to them as an example” (1 Corinthians 10:11). But the examples rest on the rescue. A youth leader had taught 1 Samuel 17 for years as a lesson in bravery, until a frightened teenager told him, “I’m not David. I’m scared all the time.” The next week he taught it again, this time pointing to Christ the champion. The boy did not become fearless, but for the first time he saw that he did not have to win his own battles alone.

For reflection

Which Old Testament story were you taught as a lesson in being good, and how does it read when you ask first what God is doing? Why do you think Scripture is so honest about its heroes’ failures? Which “true and better” comparison moves you most? Where are you in the story of David and Goliath, and what difference does that make?

16.title: Poetry, Prophecy and Wisdom
16.essay:
After the law and the stories come the songs, sermons and sayings: the Psalms, the Prophets, and the wisdom books of Job, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. They make up a large part of the Old Testament, and each kind of writing needs to be read in its own way. A love song is not a recipe; a proverb is not a contract. Learning how these books work opens them up, and they too lead us to Christ.

Hebrew poetry

English poetry often rhymes sounds. Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas. The main feature is called parallelism: a line is followed by another that echoes, sharpens or contrasts it. “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1) says the same thing twice in different words, so that it sinks in. “A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother” (Proverbs 10:1) makes its point by contrast. Once you notice it, you stop reading the second line as a new fact and start hearing the thought deepen. Poetry also uses pictures: God as rock, shepherd, shield. These are true, but they are pictures (the study Hermeneutics explains figures of speech).

The Psalms: the prayer book of Christ and the church

The Psalms are Israel’s songs and prayers, written over many centuries. They cover the whole range of the human heart: praise, thanks, confession, trust, and lament. Some psalms simply ask, “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). One, Psalm 88, ends in darkness without resolution. God put these prayers in his book, which means you may bring him your darkest feelings honestly.

Jesus said the Psalms speak of him (Luke 24:44). He prayed them. On the cross he cried out the opening of Psalm 22, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and died with words from Psalm 31 on his lips (Luke 23:46). Hebrews even puts a psalm in his mouth as he sings among his people (Hebrews 2:12). Dietrich Bonhoeffer called the Psalms the prayer book of the Bible, prayed first by Christ and then by his church with him. So when we pray the Psalms, we are not only praying for ourselves; we are joining the prayers of our Lord.

The prophets: God’s covenant prosecutors

We often think of prophets as people who predicted the future. They did, but most of their work was calling Israel back to the covenant. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 had set out blessings for faithfulness and curses for rebellion. The prophets came like lawyers bringing God’s case to court: “Hear, you mountains, the indictment of the LORD … for the LORD has an indictment against his people” (Micah 6:2). Hosea says, “the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land” (Hosea 4:1). They exposed idolatry and injustice, warned of judgment, and then, astonishingly, promised mercy beyond judgment: “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18).

Their predictions often have a near and a far fulfilment. Isaiah gave King Ahaz a sign about a child in his own day, and Matthew saw it filled to the full in Jesus, Immanuel, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). Joel’s promise of the Spirit was fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–17). The prophets saw the future like a traveller seeing distant mountain peaks: two peaks can look like one until you walk between them. Peter says the prophets themselves “searched and inquired carefully” about the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow (1 Peter 1:10–11).

Some prophecy, especially in Daniel and parts of Ezekiel and Zechariah, is apocalyptic: visions of beasts, horns, rivers and cities. These are symbols, and Scripture often explains them: “These four great beasts are four kings” (Daniel 7:17). Read them as pictures of real powers and of God’s final victory, not as coded newspaper headlines.

Wisdom: Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes

Proverbs teaches skill for living in God’s world, and it begins with God: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). But proverbs are general truths, not promises. “Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6) describes how things usually go; it is not a guarantee that every child of godly parents will believe. Proverbs itself shows this by putting two sayings side by side: “Answer not a fool according to his folly … Answer a fool according to his folly” (Proverbs 26:4–5). Wisdom is knowing which one fits the moment.

Job and Ecclesiastes keep us from turning Proverbs into a machine. Job’s friends insisted that suffering always means sin; God said they were wrong. Ecclesiastes observes that “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong” (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Life under the sun does not always add up. The three books belong together (the study Biblical Wisdom explores them).

And wisdom has a face. Jesus said, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Paul calls him “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), the one “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

A woman struggling with depression found she could not pray in her own words. Her pastor encouraged her to keep seeing her doctor, and gave her the Psalms of lament to pray. She was surprised that God had given words for exactly how she felt. Slowly she found that Psalm 42 did not stay in the dark either: “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him” (Psalm 42:5).

The story that needs him, and finds him

Stand back now from the whole Old Testament. There is a tent where God lived among his people, but the way into his presence was barred. There are priests who died one after another, and sacrifices that had to be repeated every morning and every evening. There are feasts that rehearsed a rescue still to come, laws that showed the way but could not change the heart, kings who failed, prophets who looked ahead, and wise men who reached the edge of what they knew. Every part of it is incomplete. Every part is leaning forward.

Then the book that needs him finds him. “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). He is the tabernacle where God lives among us, the mercy seat sprinkled with blood, the priest who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25), the Lamb at Passover and the firstfruits of the harvest, the law-keeper, the greater David, the true wisdom of God. The spoons and tables and curtains were not trivia. Even the humblest belonged to a house built to God’s pattern, and the whole house was his careful sketch of his Son. And the story ends where the tabernacle was always pointing, with God dwelling with his people, where “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). Read the Old Testament with him in view, and you will find that from beginning to end, “it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39).

For reflection

How does knowing about parallelism change the way you read a psalm? Which psalm could you pray this week as a prayer that Christ himself prayed? Why is it important to read Proverbs as wisdom rather than promises? Looking back over this study, where in the Old Testament do you now see Christ most clearly?
